slides.0.title: Terroir and style comparison, including other sparkling wines
slides.0.subtitle: Building comparison grids for blind tasting and essays
slides.1.title: Comparing the four sub-regions
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Montagne de Reims: structure and red fruit
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Pinot Noir dominates and supplies body and frame to many NVs and Blanc de Noirs; south-facing Ambonnay and Bouzy are often described as rich, north-side Verzenay and Verzy as tight and high in acidity (common descriptions, not rules)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Vallée de la Marne: fruit and roundness
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Meunier increases towards the west, adding round fruit and earlier drinkability; Aÿ is known for Pinot Noir (WineWithSeth). Meunier buds later, which suits the valley’s frost and humidity
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Côte des Blancs: precision and minerality
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Chardonnay on chalk slopes: fine, high in acid and long-lived. Cramant is often called floral and delicate, Le Mesnil tight, mineral and long-lived, Avize precise and powerful, Oger rounder (descriptive, not rules, not examined)
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Côte des Bar: ripeness, roundness, Pinot Noir
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Pinot Noir-led Aube on Kimmeridgian marl rather than chalk, often described as fuller, earlier-drinking and more fruit-forward; no village there holds Grand or Premier Cru status (Level 2)
slides.1.content: In a comparison grid keep “rule facts” (varieties, village lists, soils) apart from “customary descriptions” (style adjectives).
slides.2.title: Chalk and Kimmeridgian: linking to Burgundy
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Two different limestones
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Central Champagne (Montagne, Marne, Côte des Blancs) sits on Cretaceous chalk, while Chablis and the Côte des Bar sit on Jurassic Kimmeridgian marl (Levels 1 and 2). Distinguish them as “Cretaceous vs Jurassic” instead of lumping everything under “limestone”
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Cross-reference to the Burgundy course
slides.2.highlights.1.content: The Burgundy course’s Chablis lesson covers Kimmeridgian soil and Chardonnay as a still wine; its Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune lessons cover Pinot Noir and Chardonnay as still wines. This lesson only asks what the same grape and soil become as sparkling wine; revisit those lessons for soil detail, which is not repeated here
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Cool climate and high acidity
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Both share a cool northern climate and high acidity; the difference is that Champagne base wine is picked at lower sugar and higher acidity on purpose for the second fermentation, while still Chablis seeks full ripeness. Same grape, different harvest goal, different style
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Where the Côte des Bar sits
slides.2.highlights.3.content: The Côte des Bar lies about 130 km from the centre of Champagne and shares the Kimmeridgian belt with Chablis (Level 2); in blind tastings sparkling wines from Kimmeridgian soils often seem rounder and more fruit-forward. That is a style observation, not an identification rule
slides.2.content: Linking to existing lessons avoids rewriting, saves memory load and prevents contradictions.
slides.3.title: Blanc de Blancs, Blanc de Noirs and blends
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Blanc de Blancs
slides.3.highlights.0.content: White grapes only (in practice Chardonnay, though the specification also allows Arbane, Petit Meslier and other white varieties). Style: citrus, white blossom, minerality and high acidity, reserved when young and opening to cream and toast with age; the Côte des Blancs is the heartland
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Blanc de Noirs
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Black grapes only (Pinot Noir, Meunier). Style: red fruit and fuller body and texture; Pinot Noir-led wines have more structure and ageing frame, Meunier-led wines are rounder and earlier. The white juice comes from gentle whole-bunch pressing of black grapes (Level 2)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: The value of blending
slides.3.highlights.2.content: A typical NV blends three varieties, several villages and several vintages: Chardonnay’s acidity and finesse, Pinot Noir’s structure and Meunier’s fruit and softness complement one another (Level 1). Single-variety or single-village wines express place; blends pursue balance and consistency — two different philosophies
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Two roads to rosé
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Champagne rosé can come from direct pressing, skin contact or saignée, or from blending still white and red wine before bottling; blending is the Champagne speciality, with red wine commonly around 5–20% (Comité Champagne, Level 2). In the glass, blended rosé tends to be paler and softer, skin-contact rosé deeper and more structured
slides.3.content: DGCCRF: if “Blanc de Blancs”, “Blanc de Noirs” or a single variety is stated, 100% of the grapes must match (the general rule is 85%).
slides.4.title: Traditional-method neighbours: Cava, Franciacorta, England and Tasmania
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Cava: warm sites, native grapes, tiers by ageing
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Traditional-method sparkling wine centred on the Penedès, built on native grapes such as Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada. Minimum ageing: Cava 9 months, Reserva 18, Gran Reserva 30, Paraje Calificado 36 (Glass of Bubbly). Against Champagne: a warmer climate and lower-acid base wines, with a style leaning to texture and Mediterranean character
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Franciacorta: Chardonnay by the lake
slides.4.highlights.1.content: A Lombardy DOCG led by Chardonnay with Pinot Nero second; Lake Iseo moderates temperatures. Minimum lees time from tirage: standard 18 months, Satèn and Rosé 24, Millesimato 30, Riserva 60 (WineWithSeth), with yields capped at about 10 tonnes/ha. Softer mousse and riper fruit than Champagne’s tense acidity
slides.4.highlights.2.title: England: a continuation of the same chalk belt
slides.4.highlights.2.content: WineWithSeth notes that the South Downs chalk of Sussex shares belemnite chalk with the Côte des Blancs. Under the PDO rules, traditional-method sparkling needs at least nine months on lees and may use Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier. A record 21.6 million bottles were made in the UK in 2023, mostly traditional method (WineWithSeth; a yearly figure, not examined). Southern England is cooler and more northerly, with high acidity
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Tasmania: a cool island in the south
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Tasmania is Australia’s southernmost and coolest wine region, maritime with a mean January temperature of about 15.6°C, and Chardonnay and Pinot Noir lead its traditional-method sparkling (WineWithSeth). Compared with Champagne: stronger sunshine, no chalk, and styles that are usually more fruit-forward with bright acidity. Check regional data for specifics
slides.4.content: The ageing figures come from single sources and DO/DOCG rules get revised; they are comparison material here, outside the quiz, and should be checked against official specifications before an exam.
slides.5.title: Crémant, Prosecco and telling them apart blind
slides.5.highlights.0.title: Crémant: France’s family of traditional-method AOCs
slides.5.highlights.0.content: Also bottle-fermented, hand-harvested and whole-bunch pressed, spread across AOCs including Alsace, Bourgogne, Loire, Bordeaux, Limoux, Die, Jura and Savoie (WineWithSeth). Minimum lees ageing differs by AOC (sources quote 9 or 12 months among others) and bottle pressure is lower than Champagne (about 4 bar versus 5–6), none of which is examined. For Loire, see the Loire course
slides.5.highlights.1.title: Prosecco: tank method (Charmat)
slides.5.highlights.1.content: Typical tank-method second fermentation (grape: Glera) in a closed tank, which preserves primary fruit and floral aromas, gives a coarser mousse, is usually drunk young and costs less. Unlike traditional method it lacks the bread and brioche notes from autolysis, which is the key blind-tasting clue
slides.5.highlights.2.title: The first cut in blind tasting
slides.5.highlights.2.content: Steps: mousse and colour → autolysis or not (traditional vs tank) → acidity and ripeness (cool vs warm origin) → grape clues (green apple and citrus = Chardonnay; red fruit = Pinot Noir; round fruit = Meunier or a warmer origin) → level of age
slides.5.highlights.3.title: How to write the comparison grid
slides.5.highlights.3.content: Use fixed columns: climate, main varieties, soil, method and ageing, typical style, price position. Date and source every number and mark style words as “common descriptions”. The same grid serves blind-tasting reasoning and MW essays
slides.5.content: The aim is not to memorise other regions’ numbers but to explain why Champagne’s acidity, autolysis and ageing look the way they do.
slides.6.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Which statement about the soils of central Champagne versus Chablis and the Côte des Bar is correct?
A. All three are the same chalk
B. Central Champagne is Kimmeridgian and Chablis is chalk
C. Central Champagne is Cretaceous chalk; Chablis and the Côte des Bar are Jurassic Kimmeridgian marl
D. All three are volcanic soils
This distinction was set in Levels 1 and 2: compare as “Cretaceous versus Jurassic”.
On a Champagne label, what does “Blanc de Noirs” mean?
A. A white wine made only from black grapes
C. Made only from white grapes
D. Produced only in the Aube
DGCCRF: Blanc de noirs uses black grapes only; Blanc de blancs uses white grapes only.
Which sparkling wine is most typically made by the tank (Charmat) method?
Champagne, Franciacorta and Cava are bottle-fermented (traditional method); Prosecco is typically tank-method.
